I come from a very musical family. My parents believed in starting music lessons at a very early age. All of my brothers and sisters were exceptional musicians. I was not.

If my family hadn't been so musical, would I have been subjected to piano lessons? If my teacher hadn't given up on me, would my mother have decided to teach me? If mother had realized how much I hated playing, would she have released me sooner? Honestly, if had known from the beginning it could turn out well, I would have been stunned.

I have no love for the piano or music. I remember each lesson as a special torture. I was sitting there, forlorn. I was trying to play Bach. My mother was sitting beside me on the stool, patiently correcting me. Finally, I told her I had no talent. I never knew when I hit a wrong note!

Mother was smiling her lovely smile. She said it was fine and that I would learn. I said I was playing without feeling because I felt nothing.

If we had gone on like that much longer, we would have both been miserable. If I hadn't been honest, saying I wanted no more lessons, it would have continued and continued.

Then we both realized she hated giving me music lessons as much as I hated taking them. We decided then and there that I wasn't a musician. I am happy to report that I have not touched a musical instrument since!

The Simple Present, The Simple Past and The Past Continuous Tenses
When you tell stories and anecdotes, it is common to use a mixture of tenses. That allows you to convey a variety of timelines and action sequences.
You use the Simple Present tense to talk about permanent situations or about things that happen regularly.

I come from a very musical family.
I remember each lesson as a special torture.
I practice every day.
You use the Simple Past tense to talk about many kinds of past events: short, quickly finished actions, longer situations and repeated events.

Finally, I told her I had no talent.
I never knew when I hit a wrong note!
You use the Past Continuous tense to talk about an action that was happening at a time before now and to describe the background in a story written in the past tense.
I was sitting there, forlorn. I was trying to play Bach. My mother was sitting beside me on the stool, patiently correcting me.
• Remember that you cannot use the Past Continuous tense with “stative” verbs (non-action).

For example:
I was loving her.
She was being there.
I have no love for the piano or music.
I remember each lesson as a special torture.
I was sitting there, forlorn.
I was trying to play Bach. My mother was sitting beside me on the stool, patiently correcting me.
Finally, I told her I had no talent.
I never knew when I hit a wrong note!
Mother was smiling her lovely smile.
She said it was fine and that I would learn.
I said I was playing without feeling because I felt nothing.
The Third Conditional - Talking Hypothetically About the Past
You use the third conditional to talk about unreal situations in the past. These are things that did not happen in the past. You often use the third conditional to speculate about the past.
When you want to talk about situations in the past in a hypothetical context (not real or necessarily true), you can use the structure would have + past participle.
If my family hadn't been so musical, would I have been subjected to piano lessons?
